A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RTC research. Their main text, equations, algorithms, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite reorganization and added material in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original Kinetix simulation results, six real-world robot experiments, ablations, and latency measurements in Section 5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments in Section 4 and adds masking and inpainting comparisons and component-level latency measurements in Appendices A.3–A.4.

M1.justification: RTC retains the same guided inpainting, guidance clipping, exponential soft masking, delay estimation, and asynchronous execution procedures. Equations 1–5 and Algorithm 1 are unchanged in substance; the additional masking and inpainting variants are evaluated as alternatives.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 12 Kinetix environments and six real-world manipulation tasks, including two mobile tasks. The added appendix comparisons use existing coverage and introduce no new task, domain, or input-environment scenario.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 8 adds an evaluated comparator using Diffuser's overwrite-based inpainting procedure; v1 only discusses and cites Diffuser. The original simulated and real-world comparator sets remain in their corresponding main experiments.

E3.justification: v2 Table 3 adds component-level profiling of vanilla π0.5 and RTC, separating image encoding, LLM prefill, and denoising. This extends the measurement procedure alongside the retained latency comparisons. The original training budgets, horizons, rollout settings, and injected delays remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1 already analyzes hard versus soft masking, execution horizon, inference delay, and guidance clipping. v2 Appendix A.4 adds linear and no-decay masking schedules and a comparison of overwrite-based versus guided inpainting. Table 3 additionally locates the computational overhead within model inference. These are focused extensions of existing analyses.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports that its new component-level timing results use one profiling trace per method, without an uncertainty estimate. This adds limited replication information for the new analysis. Existing seed counts, Wilson intervals, SEM bars, and latency standard deviations are retained; no increase in repeated runs is reported.

E6.justification: v2 Figure 8 newly reports that exponential masking performs best overall, linear decay is close, and Diffuser-style inpainting trails RTC. Table 3 reports 18 ms for image encoding and 44 ms for prefill with either method, while five denoising steps take 14 ms without RTC and 35 ms with RTC. The original principal performance plots and latency values are retained.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and timing constraints remain unchanged. v2's explicit real-time explanation and d ≤ H − s condition elaborate the existing framework and Figure 3 constraint. Neither version presents theoretical results or proofs, and no substantive derivation or mathematical correction is added.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same contributions: training-free asynchronous execution for diffusion/flow policies, the dynamic Kinetix benchmark, and improved latency robustness and robot throughput. The additional evidence does not redefine or expand these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 newly explains when action chunking forms the outer loop of cascade control and why that interpretation does not cover its directly force-controlled simulations. Section 6 also characterizes computational overhead more strongly and explicitly identifies diffusion/flow-only applicability as a limitation.

D1.justification: v2 adds profiling details identifying the SigLIP image encoders and Gemma 2B prefill components. Its checklist explicitly discloses that π0.5 training data and real-robot runtime code are proprietary and unreleased, and states Kinetix's MIT license. Existing hyperparameters, hardware descriptions, compute budgets, and simulated-code access information are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Coughanowr and LeBlanc's cascade-control reference and a paragraph connecting that literature to action chunking. It also strengthens the distinction from model-based MPC and links the existing Diffuser discussion to an actual comparison. The remaining cited works and central novelty positioning are retained.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 5, parts of the timing discussion are rewritten, and a NeurIPS checklist and conference header are added. Most of the abstract, introduction, method description, and experimental narrative remains unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds the masking/inpainting plots in Figure 8 and the profiling table, removes v1's six-task photographic montage, and relocates or renumbers retained displays. Algorithm 1 is split across two pages. These are localized display and layout changes rather than a broad visual redesign.

improvement.justification: The added masking-schedule tests and evaluated Diffuser alternative provide useful support for design choices that v1 justified less directly. Component profiling and clearer access and applicability limitations improve transparency. These gains outweigh the modest loss of visual task context from removing the photographic montage, while the core method and principal experimental evidence remain stable.
